title: Container Runtime, Networking & Storage
summary: How a container gets network access and persistent data, and what actually runs underneath the `docker` command.

slides.markdown:
`docker` is a friendly CLI in front of a stack of smaller, standardized pieces — a daemon, a lower-level runtime, and a spec they both agree to. Underneath, containers still need explicit setup for two things they don't get for free: **network reachability** and **data that survives a restart**.

This topic covers what's actually running below `docker`, and the concrete choices for wiring up networking and storage.

slides.subTitle: Image spec vs runtime spec
slides.markdown:
The **OCI (Open Container Initiative)** defines two separate specifications so tools can interoperate: the **image spec** (the format layers, manifests, and config must follow) and the **runtime spec** (the exact filesystem bundle and process a runtime must be able to execute).

Because both are standardized, an image built by one tool can be run by a completely different runtime, and a runtime built by one vendor can execute images from any registry — nobody has to reimplement a proprietary format.

slides.subTitle: What Docker delegates to
slides.markdown:
The `docker` CLI is the top of a delegation chain, not the whole system.

![Docker CLI delegating to containerd and runc](assets/docker-containerd-runc.svg)

`docker` talks to **containerd** (manages image pulls, storage, and container lifecycle), which calls **runc** for the actual moment of creation — the low-level tool making the `clone()`/namespace/cgroup syscalls. Kubernetes talks to containerd directly, skipping Docker entirely.

slides.subTitle: Bridge, host, none, container-to-container
slides.markdown:
| Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `bridge` (default) | Container gets its own virtual network interface on a private, NAT'd network |
| `host` | Container shares the host's network namespace directly — no isolation, no NAT |
| `none` | No networking at all |
| Container-to-container | Containers on the same user-defined bridge network can resolve each other by name |

**How to decide:** `bridge` is the safe default; `host` trades isolation for raw network performance (rare, deliberate); `none` is for workloads that shouldn't touch the network at all.

A **bridge network** is a virtual switch on the host: each container gets a virtual ethernet pair, one end inside the container's network namespace, the other plugged into the bridge. The bridge routes traffic between containers directly, and NATs outbound traffic through the host's real interface.

On a **user-defined** bridge network (as opposed to the legacy default bridge), Docker also runs embedded DNS, so containers can reach each other by container name instead of a fragile hardcoded IP.

slides.sectionTitle: Volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs
slides.subTitle: Persistence options compared
slides.markdown:
| | Volume | Bind mount | tmpfs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Managed by | Docker (lives under Docker's storage dir) | You (any host path) | Neither — lives in memory only |
| Survives container removal | Yes | Yes (it's just a host path) | No — gone on stop |
| Best for | Portable persistent data (databases) | Sharing a specific host path (config, dev source) | Sensitive or highly transient data |

**How to decide:** default to volumes for anything you want Docker to manage and back up; use bind mounts when you need a specific host path (like live-reloading source code in dev); use tmpfs when data should never touch disk at all.

slides.subTitle: A container losing its data on restart
slides.markdown:
A database container writes to `/var/lib/db-data` with no volume mounted. It works fine — until the container is removed and recreated (a routine deploy), and all the data is gone, because it lived only in that container's writable layer.

The fix: mount a named volume at that exact path (`-v db-data:/var/lib/db-data`). Now the data lives in Docker-managed storage outside any single container's lifecycle — recreating the container reattaches to the same volume and the data is untouched.

**Wrong belief:** "My app writes its data to a folder inside the container, so it must be persistent."

**Why it's wrong:** a container's writable layer is tied to that *specific container instance* — it disappears the moment the container is removed, not just stopped. Restarts of the same container are fine; recreation (which is exactly what a deploy or an orchestrator's self-healing does) wipes it.

**Correct model:** anything that must outlive a single container instance — databases, uploaded files, logs you need later — belongs on a volume or bind mount, never solely in the writable layer.

slides.subTitle: What actually runs your container
slides.markdown:
If asked "what happens underneath `docker run`," name the chain explicitly: the `docker` CLI talks to the `dockerd` daemon, which delegates to **containerd** for image and lifecycle management, which calls **runc** to actually create the namespaces and cgroups via `clone()`.

Bonus point: mention that Kubernetes talks to containerd directly through the Container Runtime Interface, without Docker in the loop at all — showing you understand the runtime layer is decoupled from any single CLI.
